html:
SMTO-HTTP-0029 — The web service took too long to respond

GUID: 16611133-3970-4468-a15e-d50882ce8310
Slug: http-timeout
Domain: HTTP · Subsystem: http

What happened

  • The web service didn't answer before SMTO's time limit. If the request was meant to change something, it may or may not have gone through.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. If the request was meant to change something (create, update, delete or send), check on the web service whether that change already happened before asking SMTO to repeat it. A timed-out request may still have reached the service, and repeating it could create a duplicate.
  2. Make sure the web service is online, and that the computer running the Gateway is switched on and connected to the network. The request travels from the Gateway to the service, so either one being unreachable causes a timeout.
  3. If the service is up but slow for this kind of request, ask SMTO to try again and give the request a longer time limit. Some large or slow requests legitimately need more time than the default wait.

What success looks like

  • SMTO shows the service's reply, and any change you asked for appears once on the service.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages SMTO. Don't turn off certificate checks or other safety settings to get past this; they don't cause timeouts.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • The HTTP request failed with a timeout (requests.Timeout or TimeoutError in the exception chain); this does not show whether the connection or the response timed out, or that the service made no change.

What this means

  • The transport exception chain contains Requests Timeout or TimeoutError; the label alone does not identify connection versus response timing or prove no remote effect. The specific receipt owns dispatch and effect truth. Authentication exchanges, resource requests and Gateway admission are separate phases; rendering this explanation performs no request and never authorizes replay of an uncertain mutation.

Why this can happen

  • The transport exception chain contains Requests Timeout or TimeoutError; the label alone does not identify connection versus response timing or prove no remote effect.

How to diagnose it

  • Inspect dispatch/effect facts and the HTTP deadline before considering another request.

How to fix it

  • gateway_core/http_errors.transport_failure classifies a requests.Timeout or TimeoutError in the exception chain as http_timeout; it does not distinguish connect from read timeouts, and an already-attempted write method is marked with an unknown outcome. Check the destination service and network from the Gateway host, reconcile any write before repeating it, and raise only the supported http.request timeout_seconds (default 30, maximum 120) when a healthy request legitimately needs longer.
  • Check the destination service and network. Adjust only a supported HTTP operation timeout when a healthy request legitimately needs longer.

Retry and execution caution

  • Apply the correction and confirm the relevant state before requesting another attempt. Prior completed work remains governed by its receipts.

How to verify the fix

  • The original mutation is reconciled if necessary and a bounded current request completes within its supported timeout.

What not to do

  • Do not remove retained state or weaken trust checks to make an unavailable dependency appear healthy.

Technical notes

  • The specific receipt owns dispatch and effect truth. Authentication exchanges, resource requests and Gateway admission are separate phases; rendering this explanation performs no request and never authorizes replay of an uncertain mutation.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
